title: Body Size and Heat Exchange
question: How does size affect passive cooling, and is a faster temperature drop the same as more total heat released?

blocks.prompt: Required before observing: Which of two similar cubes, with 1 cm or 2 cm edges, will show the greater temperature drop over the same interval? Will it also release more total heat? Explain your reasoning.
blocks.text: The smaller cube may change temperature faster because of more exposed surface per volume, but a large mass may release more total energy even with a smaller drop.

blocks.prompt: Required before observing: Why match the material, starting temperature, surrounding air, exposed faces and interval? When size changes, should mass stay the same if density stays the same? What can two passive cubes not tell us about living animals?
blocks.text: Match material, initial temperature, air temperature, exposed faces and interval. With common density, the larger volume has greater mass. Living animals also generate and regulate heat, which passive blocks do not show.
Timing: Before geometry or thermal observations.

Both model cubes use the same water-like material, with assumed density 1 g/cm³ and specific heat 4.18 J/(g·°C). Specific heat describes the energy per gram for each degree of temperature change. Each starts at 40.0°C in 20.0°C air. All six faces exchange heat with the air in the same way. Probe and support effects are ignored. Setup is a paused model; one action later advances both cubes by 20 model minutes.
One supplied model per size, not repeated trials or measured animal specimens.
Areas/volumes follow supplied dimensions. Student ratios use area divided by volume; cm⁻¹ means cm² per cm³.

Small cube
Correct after feedback.

Student readings from provided synthetic model probe displays, not measured specimens. Model interval completed: 20 minutes. Setup was paused; calculations use the single 20-model-minute interval. Current unconfirmed entries stay visible.
Drop = initial − final. Average cooling rate = drop ÷ 20 minutes. Provided smooth curves follow the chosen model; endpoint dots show checked student readings from model snapshots, not real data.

Heat estimates below are model-computed from current checked readings, assumed masses and specific heat 4.18J/(g·°C). They are supplied calculations, not student-calculated or measured calorimetry. Joules(J) measure energy; degrees Celsius measure temperature.

blocks.prompt: The large cube has a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio. Does it have less total outer area?
blocks.text:
No. It has more total area, but less area for each unit of volume.
Correct! Doubling every edge multiplies area by 4 and volume by 8. The large cube has 24 cm² instead of 6 cm², but only 3 cm² per cm³ instead of 6. Correct on first recorded check.

blocks.prompt: Why can a cube cool more slowly in degrees per minute but release more total heat over the interval?
blocks.text:
Its larger mass can transfer more energy even with a smaller temperature drop.
Correct! For the same material, transferred energy depends on mass and temperature change. A temperature change alone does not give total heat. Revised after feedback.

blocks.prompt: What does the model show about living animals?
blocks.text:
One geometric influence under matched assumptions; living temperature control needs more evidence.
Correct! Animals make metabolic heat and change insulation, circulation and behavior. Geometry matters, but it does not determine body temperature by itself. Correct on first recorded check.

All sizes, readings and energy values are supplied teaching-model data, not measured cubes or animals. Setup is paused before cooling starts. Each cube is assumed to have the same temperature throughout. A chosen rule links its cooling to surface area per volume and its current temperature difference from the air. Air stays at 20°C; the rule is not fitted to a species or calibrated apparatus. It gives curved cooling, not a constant drop each minute. All faces are exposed; probe and support contact, internal temperature differences, radiation, evaporation and changes in airflow are omitted. Later heat estimates use checked rounded readings, assumed masses and specific heat; they are calculated, not measured by calorimetry. Calorimetry means measuring heat transfer. Living animals generate metabolic heat and may change insulation, blood flow, posture or behavior. They are not passive cubes. Shape, conditions and heat direction matter; hotter surroundings could warm a cooler model. One comparison cannot estimate natural variation. Diagrams are enlarged; colors and arrows explain the model. No physical heating, cube-making or probe protocol is supplied.
